vo: Before any plane leaves the gate, someone walks around it with a checklist. Fuel. Doors. Cargo. Nobody calls that red tape. They call it flying.
Software takes off every day with no check at all. A ticket is written on Tuesday, and it ships on Thursday. Nobody looks at what's on board.
Eight months later, the complaint lands. Customers' ID numbers, collected for no stated reason, and kept forever. Who approved this? Nobody knows.
And South Africa's Information Regulator is fining. One million rand for a major bank. Half a million for a college that shared personal information without a lawful reason.
So, back to the gate. Same ticket. Same Tuesday. This time, with Preflight.
First, the scanner. Preflight reads every Jira ticket as it's written, and spots personal information on board. ID numbers. Health details. Children's data.
Then, the gate. Try to start work, and the gate stays closed. The ticket gets a checklist: why you need the data, your lawful basis, and when it's deleted.
Your co-pilot, Rovo, can draft the answers. But a draft never counts until a person confirms it. AI can help. It can't approve.
Then, the control tower. Nicholas, the Information Officer, sees every waiting ticket in one place, reads the answers, and clears it for take-off.
Gate open. Now, Ben can start work.
Peel off the label, and the scanner still remembers. Change an answer after sign-off, and the clearance is cancelled.
Before landing, at Done, a second check asks for proof: a link to the updated privacy notice.
And everything goes into the flight recorder. Every answer, every approval, write-once. So when someone asks, who approved this? The answer takes ten seconds.
The checklist is yours. Start with the POPIA or GDPR pack, or let Rovo draft rules from your own policy. Nothing is enforced until an approver switches it on.
Preflight. Privacy review, before you build.
